transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Lyndi Kenyon.
Thousands of passengers are still stranded as the U.S. air travel system slowly gets
back up to speed following yesterday's nationwide ground stop.
As NPR's Joel Rose reports, aviation regulators are laying the blame for the telecom meltdown
on a federal contractor.
Foreign Secretary Sean Duffy says the massive outage that brought the U.S. aviation system
to its knees started with a routine router upgrade by contractor L3Harris Technologies.
This was an FAA system that didn't meet the moment, a contractor didn't meet the moment,
or the equipment didn't meet the moment and caused the outages.
The Federal Aviation Administration says the work was part of the transition from older
copper wire to fiber optic cable.
In a statement, L3Harris says it is supporting the FAA's investigation into what went wrong
and that it takes the impact on airlines and travelers seriously.
Joel Rose, NPR News, Washington.
The tracking site FlightAware says more than 8,000 flights into and out of the U.S. are
delayed.
That's down for more than 21,000 delays earlier today.
More than 7,000 flights were canceled.
New Orleans port officials are suing the owner of a tanker that slammed into a cruise ship
on the Mississippi River yesterday.
All 197 passengers and crew on the American Heritage cruise ship survived.
Police Chief Melanie Montroll says the life jackets made a big difference.
What contributed to that success was the readily availability of those life preservers, right,
because whether it's 10 feet of water or 200 feet, having those vests, having that population
be able to put those vests on and kind of float upriver while we've retrieved them,
I think, was the best factor of success.
The cruise ship remains on its side in the Mississippi River.
The Coast Guard says it could take weeks to remove it due to hazardous materials on the
ship.
This could delay fully reopening the river near that collision site.
Microsoft says its products are back online after a days-long outage knocked out critical
services to companies and governments around the world.
NPR's Marissa J. Lang has the story.
Two days after a massive outage shut down Microsoft products like Outlook, Teams, and
Copilot, its AI assistant, the company announced all services had been restored to its more
than 430 million customers.
The outage affected international government operations, health care services, businesses,
banks, schools, courts, and even the U.S. House of Representatives.
In a post on X Friday, the technology company said it was "deeply sorry" and described
the outage as a "technical issue."
It said Microsoft was not the victim of any cyber-attacks or rogue AI agents, but instead
blamed the failure on a network upgrade.
Marissa J. Lang, NPR News.
The outage has affected over 70 countries.
You're listening to NPR News.
Do you think Andy Warhol's 1986 self-portrait will go for more than $16 million when it's
auctioned off next Tuesday?
Then you might be interested in the latest partnership in the art world between the art
market website ArtNet and the prediction market, KALSHI.
NPR's Anastasia Sukkles reports.
ArtNet started out in 1989 as an online database to provide info on art auction sales.
Last year, it was acquired by venture capital firm Beowulf Capital.
Now ArtNet says it will help KALSHI curate the markets that users can bet on.
Critics of the deal say that art auctions already take place in a high-stakes, insular
world and that the chances of market manipulation are steep.
Some are also saying it's going to make the art world even more focused on money, not
creative expression.
The partnership was announced soon before the annual wintertime art fairs, like Miami Art
Week, commence.
Anastasia Sukkles, NPR News.
Fans celebrated the legacy of Rocky Balboa 50 years after the film Rocky with a record
breaking gathering in Philadelphia.
Hundreds gathered yesterday at the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art to break a
record for the most number of people dressed as Rocky.
The city organized events this month to honor the fictional boxer, including a sprint up
the iconic stairs of the museum and the rededication of the Rocky statue.
The 1976 film, written by Sylvester Stallone, became a cultural phenomenon and won in the
Oscar for Best Picture.
I'm Lynda Kenyon, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: FAA air travel ground stop blamed on L3Harris router upgrade; thousands of flights delayed
New Orleans port officials sue tanker owner after collision with American Heritage cruise ship
Microsoft restores Outlook, Teams, and Copilot after days-long outage it calls a network upgrade failure
ArtNet partners with prediction market Kalshi to help curate art market betting markets
Philadelphia fans set record gathering dressed as Rocky Balboa marking film's 50th anniversary
